stem: A company runs SQL Server on an Azure virtual machine that its own team set up. It plans to move the database to Azure SQL Database, a managed database service. Under the shared responsibility model, which task moves from the company to Microsoft?

choices.text: Securing the physical servers, power and cooling in the datacenter that hosts the database's hardware.
Installing patches and updates for the database engine and the operating system that the database runs on.
Deciding which employees and applications are allowed to sign in to the database and read its tables.
Making sure the customer records loaded into the database are accurate, classified and kept only as long as needed.

stem: A manager asks which security duties stay with her company no matter whether it uses IaaS, PaaS or SaaS services in Azure. Which TWO responsibilities always remain with the customer? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The accounts and identities of the people, services and devices in the company's environment.
The power supply, cooling and building access controls of the datacenters that hold the hardware.
The physical hosts and the physical network inside the Azure datacenters that run the services.
The information and data that the company stores in its cloud services and applications.
The operating systems of the servers that run each service, including their security updates.

stem: A retailer runs a private cloud in its own datacenter, and company policy says customer payment records must stay there. Each holiday season its web storefront needs far more servers than the datacenter has for a few weeks. Which cloud model fits best?

choices.text: A private cloud only, buying enough additional servers for the holiday peak and keeping them in the datacenter all year.
A public cloud only, moving the storefront and the payment records to Azure so the datacenter can be closed down.
A hybrid cloud, keeping payment records in the private cloud and adding public cloud capacity for the holiday storefront.
A multicloud setup, running the storefront on two different public cloud providers at the same time for every season.

stem: A hospital group wants cloud-style self-service for its IT resources, but no other organization may share the hardware. It plans to rent a dedicated datacenter that a hosting company operates only for the group. Which cloud model is this?

choices.text: Private cloud, because the cloud resources are used by a single organization even though a third party hosts them.
Multicloud, because the resources involve two separate companies: the hospital group and the hosting provider.
Public cloud, because the datacenter is built and maintained by a third-party company rather than by the group's own staff.
Hybrid cloud, because the hardware belongs to one company while the resources are used by a different organization.

stem: A finance director asks how moving the company's servers from its own datacenter to Azure will change the way IT spending is recorded and planned. Which statement describes the consumption-based model correctly?

choices.text: Spending becomes a fixed annual fee that Microsoft sets in advance, whatever the company actually runs during that year.
Spending becomes capital expenditure, because the company buys an Azure subscription that is depreciated over several years.
Spending stays capital expenditure, because the company must still reserve its peak capacity before resources run.
Spending becomes operational expenditure, paid for the resources used, with no up-front purchase of server hardware.

stem: A company runs a line-of-business application on one VM size in one Azure region, 24 hours a day. It expects the same size and region for the next three years and the VM must not be interrupted. Which pricing option gives the deepest discount for this usage?

choices.text: Pay-as-you-go pricing, which bills each hour the VM runs at the standard rate with no commitment and no up-front payment.
An Azure savings plan, which commits to a fixed hourly spend that applies flexibly across eligible services and regions.
Azure Reservations, which commit to a specific resource, size and region for one or three years in return for a lower price.
Azure Spot Virtual Machines, which run on unused Azure capacity at a lower price and can be evicted whenever Azure needs it back.

stem: A small insurer needs to resize each photo that customers upload with a claim. Uploads arrive at random, from none for hours to hundreds in a few minutes. The team wants to write only the resize code and not pay for idle servers. Which approach fits best?

choices.text: Azure Virtual Desktop, which gives each claims handler a cloud desktop where the photos can be resized by hand as needed.
Azure Functions, which runs the resize code when an upload event arrives and charges only for the compute time it uses.
Azure Virtual Machines in a scale set that always keeps at least two instances running and adds more when CPU usage is high.
An Azure App Service plan that hosts the resize code as a web app with a fixed number of instances running around the clock.

stem: An online ticketing site must stay usable even when a server or other component fails during a major concert sale. Which cloud benefit does this requirement describe, and how does Azure state what customers can expect from each service?

choices.text: High availability, because the site must remain available despite disruptions, and Azure states uptime guarantees per service in SLAs.
Scalability, because Azure adds resources during the sale, and each service's expected uptime is printed in its Azure Pricing Calculator estimate.
Manageability, because the site is managed through the portal and APIs, and expected uptime is shown in each subscription's usage reports.
Governance, because policies keep the site compliant during the sale, and Azure states expected uptime in each region's compliance documents.

stem: A school's enrollment portal runs on two Azure virtual machines. On enrollment day traffic jumps tenfold, and the team adds eight more identical VMs, then removes them the next week. What type of scaling is this, and what is the main cost effect?

choices.text: Vertical scaling, because the portal's capacity goes up, and the school pays a one-time charge for the extra peak capacity used.
Vertical scaling, because adding identical VMs raises the CPU and memory of the existing two, and costs stay fixed afterwards.
Horizontal scaling, because it changes the size of each existing VM, and costs stay higher until the reserved capacity expires.
Horizontal scaling, because it adds and removes resource instances, and the school pays for the extra VMs only while they run.

stem: An architect explains that their order system is spread across several Azure regions, so that if one region suffers a disaster, the system recovers and keeps working from the others. Which cloud benefit is she describing?

choices.text: Predictability, which is the ability to forecast how much the system will cost and how it will perform in the coming months.
Governance, which is the ability to make sure that every deployed resource meets the company's technical and legal standards.
Reliability, which is the ability of a system to recover from failures and continue to function as users need it to.
Manageability, which is the ability to control the system through the portal, the CLI, APIs and PowerShell from anywhere.

stem: A retail company wants its online store to give customers consistently fast responses during unpredictable traffic, as part of the cloud benefit called performance predictability. Which TWO cloud capabilities support performance predictability? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The Azure Pricing Calculator, which estimates the monthly cost of the resources before they are deployed.
Load balancing, which spreads incoming traffic so that no single resource is overloaded by requests.
Resource tags, which label each resource with a cost center so that cloud spend can be split by team.
Usage tracking, which records resource consumption in real time so that future spend can be forecast.
Autoscaling, which adds resources when demand rises and removes them again when the demand drops.

stem: A bank must prove that every resource it deploys in Azure meets its technical standards and regulatory rules, and it wants to find any resource that drifts out of compliance. Which cloud capabilities describe the security and governance benefit it relies on?

choices.text: A multicloud setup that copies each resource to a second provider, plus cloud bursting that adds capacity on demand.
Templates that deploy resources to a defined standard, plus cloud-based auditing that flags resources out of compliance.
Vertical scaling that gives each resource more CPU and memory, plus horizontal scaling that adds instances during peak periods.
Spot pricing that runs resources on unused capacity, plus reservations that lock in a lower rate for compliant resources.

stem: Microsoft describes two kinds of manageability in the cloud: management of the cloud and management in the cloud. Which example belongs to management in the cloud?

choices.text: A new test environment is created from a preconfigured template, so that nobody has to configure its resources by hand.
A web app automatically adds more instances when its demand grows and then removes them again once the demand drops off.
A monitoring rule detects a failing resource in the environment and automatically replaces it with a new, healthy copy.
An administrator handles the company's Azure resources through the web portal, the command line, APIs and PowerShell.

stem: A manufacturer must move an old inventory application to Azure within a month. The application needs a specific operating system version and custom software installed on the server, and there is no time to redesign it. Which service type and Azure service fit best?

choices.text: IaaS, with Azure Virtual Machines where the company installs and controls the operating system and the software.
PaaS, with Azure App Service hosting the application on a platform whose operating system Microsoft manages.
PaaS, with Azure Functions running the application's code each time an inventory event arrives from the factory.
SaaS, buying a ready-made inventory application that the vendor runs and updates for all of its many customers.

stem: A three-person development team builds a web API in Python. They want to deploy code straight from their Git repository and get automatic scaling and high availability, without patching or licensing any operating system. Which option fits best?

choices.text: Azure Virtual Machines, where the team installs Python and a web server and then applies OS updates on its own schedule.
Microsoft 365, where the team publishes the web API inside the company's existing productivity apps for all of its users.
Azure App Service, a PaaS offering that hosts web apps and APIs while Microsoft maintains the platform beneath the code.
Azure Virtual Desktop, where each developer runs the API on a cloud desktop that can be reached from anywhere they work.

stem: A ten-person law firm has no IT staff. It needs email, calendars and document editing for every employee, and wants the provider to handle the servers, the application updates and their availability. Which approach fits best?

choices.text: SaaS, subscribing to a finished application such as Microsoft 365 that the firm simply signs in to and uses.
Private cloud, buying servers for a small on-site datacenter and installing mail and document software on them.
PaaS, writing its own mail and document application and hosting it on Azure App Service for the whole firm.
IaaS, running mail and document servers on Azure virtual machines that the firm configures and patches on its own.

stem: A company moves several servers to Azure virtual machines, an IaaS service. The IT team asks which duties it now has to carry out itself rather than Microsoft. Which TWO are the customer's responsibilities in IaaS? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Providing the physical security of the datacenter buildings and of the server racks inside them.
Keeping the datacenter's network connection to the internet available for all virtual machines.
Maintaining the physical hardware on which the virtual machines run inside the Azure datacenter.
Installing, configuring and patching the operating systems that run inside the virtual machines.
Configuring the virtual networks, subnets and network settings that the virtual machines will use.

stem: A consultant compares cloud service options for a client. Which option does Microsoft describe as the least flexible, but the easiest to get up and running and the one needing the least technical expertise?

choices.text: Infrastructure as a service (IaaS), because the provider hands over ready-made virtual machines with nothing else to set up.
Software as a service (SaaS), because the customer uses a fully developed application that the provider runs and maintains.
Serverless computing, because the provider runs event-driven code and the customer never sees or manages any servers.
Platform as a service (PaaS), because the provider maintains the operating system so that developers only deploy code.

stem: A company uses Microsoft 365 (SaaS). A former employee could still read shared files two weeks after leaving, because nobody disabled her account. The CIO asks whether this was Microsoft's failure under the shared responsibility model. What is the correct answer?

choices.text: Yes, because Microsoft runs the sign-in platform, so it is responsible for every account in the company's tenant and its use.
No, because user accounts are only a customer duty in IaaS, and this failure came from a datacenter problem on Microsoft's side.
No, because in SaaS the customer still manages its users and their access, while Microsoft runs the authentication platform.
Yes, because in SaaS the provider manages the whole stack, so Microsoft must remove accounts when employees leave a company.

stem: A company is planning four projects in Azure. For which project is platform as a service (PaaS) the most appropriate service type?

choices.text: Moving a legacy accounting server that depends on a custom kernel driver to Azure without changing any of its code.
Building a new customer portal on a managed platform that already includes built-in scaling and high availability.
Giving all staff a ready-made email and calendar service that they can start using right away with only a web browser.
Running a test lab where engineers install different operating system versions and reconfigure each one as needed.

stem: A small company plans to move a web app to Azure next quarter. Before anything is deployed, the owner wants a monthly cost estimate for an App Service plan, a managed database and storage, compared across two regions. Which tool should they use?

choices.text: Azure Advisor cost recommendations, which find underused resources in an existing subscription
A Cost Management budget, which sends an alert when actual spending passes a set threshold
Cost analysis in Microsoft Cost Management, which breaks down the charges of resources already running
The Azure pricing calculator, which models the planned services and options without deploying anything

stem: A team created a monthly budget in Microsoft Cost Management for its dev subscription with an alert at 100%. Spending passed the budget, the team received an email, but every VM kept running. What explains this?

choices.text: The budget failed because budgets apply only to resource groups and cannot be scoped to a whole subscription
The VMs kept running because a resource lock on the subscription overrides the budget's stop action
A budget only notifies when thresholds are reached; resources keep running unless an action group runs automation
Budgets stop resources only for production subscriptions, so the dev subscription was treated as exempt

stem: A company compares two deployment options and sees different monthly costs for what looks like the same workload. Which TWO factors can change the cost of Azure resources? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The region where the resources are deployed, because prices can differ between regions
Management groups placed above the subscriptions to organise policy and access
Tags attached to each resource for cost reporting and ownership tracking
How many resource groups the same resources are spread across in the subscription
Outbound data transfer leaving Azure datacenters, which is priced by billing zone

stem: Several departments share one resource group that holds a single application, and the resources cannot be split up. Finance wants monthly cost reports per department. What is the simplest approach?

choices.text: Create a management group for each department and move the shared resource group under all of them
Place a resource lock on each department's resources so their charges appear on a separate invoice
Assign an Azure Policy initiative per department so that compliance reports also show each team's spending
Apply a CostCenter tag to each resource and group the costs by that tag in Cost Management cost analysis

stem: An admin tagged a resource group with Environment=Prod. Later, cost analysis grouped by the Environment tag shows the VMs and disks inside that group as untagged. What is the reason?

choices.text: Resources do not inherit resource group tags, so tag each resource, for example by using Azure Policy
Tags take effect only on resources created by ARM templates, so resources made in the portal stay untagged
Tags on a resource group appear in cost analysis only after a resource lock is also applied to that group
Tag values are case-sensitive, so cost analysis ignores any tag whose name begins with an uppercase letter

stem: Admins of a production storage account must keep changing its settings, but nobody, including Owners, should be able to delete it by accident. Which control fits best?

choices.text: An Azure Policy assignment with the Allowed locations rule set to the storage account's current region
The Reader role for every admin on the storage account, so they can view it but not remove it
A Delete (CanNotDelete) resource lock on the storage account, which blocks deletion but allows changes
A ReadOnly resource lock on the storage account, which blocks deletion and keeps the settings editable

stem: A user with the Owner role tries to resize a VM and gets an error. The VM's resource group has a ReadOnly lock. What must happen before the resize can succeed?

choices.text: An Azure Policy remediation task must run, because locks are released when a policy marks resources compliant
The lock must be removed first, because locks apply to every user regardless of their role assignment
Microsoft support must approve the change, because only support can modify resources under a ReadOnly lock
The user must also be given the User Access Administrator role, which allows actions on locked resources

stem: A European company must make sure that no team can create Azure resources outside two approved EU regions, in every subscription. Which service should enforce this?

choices.text: Resource locks of type ReadOnly on each subscription, so that resources cannot be placed in other regions
Azure Policy, assigning the Allowed locations definition at a scope above the subscriptions
Microsoft Purview, scanning the subscriptions and classifying data stored outside the approved regions
Microsoft Defender for Cloud, which builds the approved region list from the subscription's secure score

stem: A retailer keeps data in Azure SQL Database, in on-premises SQL Server and in Amazon S3. Compliance staff need one map of where sensitive data is, with classification and lineage. Which service should they use?

choices.text: Microsoft Purview, for automated data discovery, classification and lineage across the whole estate
Azure Arc, which projects the S3 buckets and SQL servers into Azure and labels the sensitive columns
Azure Policy, which inspects the rows in each database and assigns a sensitivity label to each table
Azure Monitor Log Analytics, which collects data from all three sources into one workspace for queries

stem: A company assigns a new Azure Policy that allows only certain VM sizes. Some VMs created last year use a size not on the list. How does Azure Policy treat those existing VMs?

choices.text: It applies a ReadOnly lock to them, so that nobody can change them until they meet the new rule
It deletes them automatically, because Deny policies remove every resource that breaks the rule
It ignores them permanently, because a policy only ever applies to resources created after assignment
It evaluates them and reports them as noncompliant; they keep running unless the company remediates them

stem: An administrator works from a shared kiosk PC where installing software is blocked. They need to run a few Azure CLI commands against their subscription today. What should they use?

choices.text: An ARM template uploaded to a storage account, which runs the CLI commands when a file is added
Azure Arc, which connects the kiosk PC to Azure so commands can be run against the subscription
Azure Cloud Shell, a browser-based shell that is already authenticated and ships with the Azure CLI
Azure PowerShell installed locally on the kiosk PC, which provides the same commands as the Azure CLI

stem: A company runs Windows and Linux servers in its own datacenter and Kubernetes clusters in another public cloud. It wants to see them in Azure and apply the same Azure Policy rules it uses for Azure resources. Which service enables this?

choices.text: Azure Migrate, which discovers the on-premises servers and keeps managing them where they currently run
Azure ExpressRoute, which connects the datacenter to Azure so Azure Policy can reach the servers
Azure Arc, which projects servers and Kubernetes clusters outside Azure into Azure Resource Manager
Azure Site Recovery, which replicates the servers to Azure so they can be governed as Azure resources

stem: A team notices that a VM created in the Azure portal, with the Azure CLI or with Azure PowerShell behaves the same and obeys the same permissions. Why is that?

choices.text: Every request is approved by Azure Advisor, which checks it against best practices before deployment
Every request is first stored in Azure Monitor, which replays it to the resource in the same order
Every request runs inside Azure Cloud Shell, which converts portal clicks into the same Azure CLI commands
Every request from these tools goes to Azure Resource Manager, which authenticates and authorizes it

stem: A team must build identical dev, test and production environments many times a year. They want to describe the desired end state in files kept in source control and let Azure handle deployment order. What should they use?

choices.text: Bicep files deployed through Azure Resource Manager as declarative infrastructure as code
Step-by-step portal instructions in a wiki that each engineer follows for every new environment
Resource locks set on the dev environment and copied to test and production by Azure Policy
Azure Advisor recommendations exported to source control and replayed for each new environment

stem: A company moves from scripted, step-by-step deployments to ARM templates. Which TWO benefits of ARM templates should it expect? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Enforcement: after deployment the template blocks every manual portal change to the deployed resources
Declarative syntax: the template states which resources should exist instead of listing commands to run
Isolation: each template can contain only one resource, which keeps every deployment small and simple
Scope: a template can deploy only to the region of the subscription that the deploying user signed in from
Orchestration: Azure Resource Manager works out dependency order and deploys resources in parallel where it can

stem: A startup wants personalized suggestions to reduce spending on underused VMs and to improve the reliability and security of its existing Azure resources. Which service should it check?

choices.text: Azure Advisor, which evaluates existing resources and recommends changes for cost, reliability and more
Azure Service Health, which reports outages and planned maintenance for the Azure services and regions in use
The Azure pricing calculator, which estimates the cost of resources and options before they are deployed
Microsoft Purview, which scans the subscriptions and recommends cheaper storage tiers for classified data

stem: An operations team wants to be alerted automatically about outages and planned maintenance that affect the specific Azure services and regions it uses, not every Azure event worldwide. Which should it set up?

choices.text: A Cost Management budget alert, which emails the team when costs grow because of an Azure outage
Service Health alerts, based on a personalized view of the Azure services and regions the team uses
The Azure status page, which shows the health of all Azure services in all regions for every customer
Azure Advisor notifications, which report new recommendations to improve the configuration of resources

stem: Developers of a web app running partly in Azure and partly on-premises want to see request rates, response times, failure rates and slow dependency calls, and to test from outside that the site responds. What should they use?

choices.text: Azure Resource Health, which reports per-request response times and failures for each web server
Microsoft Cost Management cost analysis, which traces slow requests through their resource charges
Application Insights, which monitors web app performance and usage and supports availability tests
Azure Advisor performance recommendations, which measure response times for every request served

stem: Azure Monitor already collects logs from 40 VMs. An engineer needs to find every error event logged across all of them in the last hour and chart the trend over the past week. Which tool should they use?

choices.text: The Azure status page, which shows the errors from all VMs in a subscription for the selected period
Azure Resource Health, which lists the error events written by the operating system of each VM
Azure Advisor, which groups the error events of all VMs into recommendations sorted by severity
Log Analytics in the Azure portal, which runs queries against the log data that Azure Monitor collects

stem: An admin wants an SMS sent to the on-call engineer whenever a VM's CPU stays above 80% for 10 minutes. Which TWO Azure Monitor components are needed? (Select TWO)

choices.text: A Delete resource lock on the VM, so that Azure Monitor can read its CPU metrics continuously
An alert rule with a metric condition on the VM's CPU percentage over the 10-minute period
A Service Health alert that fires when Azure reports maintenance on the VM's host in the region
A Cost Management budget with a threshold based on the VM's forecasted compute spending
An action group that defines who is notified, such as the on-call engineer's phone number
